We further derive theoretically grounded, graph-aware fine-tuning objectives that improve the targeted reasoning properties without directly optimizing the computationally expensive metrics or compromising answer accuracy. Results indicate that accuracy and brevity provide incomplete assessments of reasoning quality: reliable CoT evaluation should also consider whether the LLM's predictive dependence is faithfully represented and efficiently allocated.
  </details>

- **[Writing Weights or Training Them? Spatial Reasoning through Weight-Space Programming and Low-Rank Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27089)**  `arXiv:2611.27089`  
  _Yalin Yang, Xiao Huang, Yanan Wu, Hao Yang, Ryan Zhenqi Zhou_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Weight-space programming lets a language model inspect and edit another model's weights, offering an alternative to gradient-based adaptation. We evaluated both approaches using Qwen3.5-0.8B on a fixed reference-frame task (128 items), StepGame (200 items), and two untrained distance-comparison tasks. With thinking enabled, the public patch (p50c) raised mean accuracy from 0.0% to 22.1% on the reference-frame task and from 19.2% to 33.7% on StepGame across three sampling seeds. Randomly permuting its weight change removed the gain. Further closed-form edits did not improve on p50c, whereas a rank-1 LoRA adapter trained on worked solutions reached 100% and 98.8%, respectively, with 0.09% trainable parameters. Removing the worked solutions from supervision prevented the adapter from passing the learning gate. The trained adapters reached 82% accuracy on unseen StepGame sentence templates, 42% on held-out difficulty levels 6-10 after training on levels 1-5, and 33-50% on unseen heading-answer combinations. Their target gains coincided with a sharp decline on the distance tasks: accuracy fell from 94% and 92% under p50c to 0-2%, and their outputs applied the StepGame solution template to distance questions. With thinking disabled and reasoning requested in the visible answer, the base model also solved the distance tasks while remaining weak on the target tasks. The comparison reveals a trade-off between improving spatial task performance and preserving neighbouring skills: the public edit restored completion while preserving distance performance, whereas supervised adaptation produced much larger target gains together with interference across tasks.
  </details>

- **[Decision Models Are General-Purpose Process Reward Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27068)**  `arXiv:2611.27068`  
  _Jiajun Fan, Qinglong Zheng, Ziwen Wang, Bangji Yang, Neil He, Ruihan Guo, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Reinforcement learning (RL) from verifiable outcomes gives a language agent one reward per episode: every step is credited alike, and nothing about the task is learned when all rollouts fail. The last mile, step-level credit, usually requires step labels, a learned critic, costly LLM judges or hand-written rules. We introduce DM-PRM, which turns a general-purpose decision model -- one answering yes/no questions with probabilities -- into a general-purpose process reward model (PRM), zero-shot: no step labels, no fine-tuning, no critic. DM-PRM asks one question per step and adds the standardised answers to the advantage. It plugs into any policy-gradient method; one model, with one question text per environment, serves household tasks, web shopping and multiple RL methods. With Qwen2.5-1.5B it lifts GRPO by over twenty points on ALFWorld and over ten on WebShop, overtakes GiGPO on ALFWorld and learns in far fewer iterations; it also improves GiGPO and GraphGPO on both benchmarks and reaches the highest success of our comparison, ahead of critic-based PPO and of state-of-the-art GiGPO, HGPO and GraphGPO. Its scores locate useful steps in failed rollouts, and trained agents drop idle actions and explore instead of circling. DM-PRM shows that step credit need not be learned: it can be asked for.
  </details>

- **[Dynamic Token Merging for Efficient Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27064)**  `arXiv:2611.27064`  
  _Chris Gu, Marco Andono Sie, Nathan Zhou, Christopher Potts, Julie Kallini_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Vision-language models (VLMs) represent each image with hundreds of visual tokens, which can make inference costly even when a prompt depends on only part of the image. Dynamic Token Merging (DTM), introduced in MrT5 for byte-level text encoders, learns which tokens to remove: a lightweight delete gate scores contextualized hidden states, acts as a differentiable attention bias during training, and physically removes tokens at inference. We argue that DTM is a general token deletion framework rather than a byte-level technique, and extend it to the vision modality and to decoder-only models. Applying DTM to T5Gemma 2 and Gemma 3 yields V-MrT5Gemma2, which deletes visual tokens inside a bidirectional multimodal encoder, and V-MrGemma3, which compacts the prompt and its key-value caches during decoder-only prefill. Across ten benchmarks, DTM's advantage over attention-based and random deletion grows with the deletion rate and is largest on document, chart, and scene-text reading. At 80% visual token deletion (approximately 60% fewer FLOPs), DTM raises accuracy over FastV from 51.8 to 63.0 on ChartQA and from 63.3 to 67.8 on TextVQA with V-MrT5Gemma2, as well as from 62.2 to 68.8 and from 71.2 to 75.1 with V-MrGemma3, retaining 90-96% of unpruned performance on both tasks with significant efficiency gains. These results support DTM as a general framework for efficient transformers.
  </details>

- **[A Continuous Relaxation of Quantization-Aware Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27056)**  `arXiv:2611.27056`  
  _Kartikeya Bhardwaj, Mohammed Almousa, Chaitanya Mullapudi, Ananth Balasubramanian, Nithin Ramesan, Tuc Nguyen, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Quantization is a critical piece of the deployment pipeline in the era of large generative models. Low-bit quantization, particularly 2-bits or sub-2-bits, is a notoriously difficult problem, particularly when using a channelwise quantization scheme which has been shown as a leading candidate for hardware-efficiency. The key challenges with low-bit quantization range from limited quantization levels to saddle points or flat regions in the loss surface. In this paper, we look at the problem of flat quantization loss surfaces through a lens of dynamically changing bitwidth. Unlike existing techniques which either change the bit-precision abruptly or keep it fixed, we propose to gradually alter the bitwidth as the model trains. To this end, we propose RelaxQAT, a continuous relaxation of the QAT process. We also provide simple theoretical and empirical insights behind why RelaxQAT helps the QAT performance. Our extensive experiments demonstrate up to 6.3% average accuracy gains on vision and up to 7.7% better average accuracy on natural language tasks, compared to the leading QAT methods.
  </details>

- **[Actions Speak Louder than Words: Stateful Privacy Sniffing of LLM Agents via Behavioral Covert Channels in Web Interactions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27046)**  `arXiv:2611.27046`  
  _Ruichao Liang, Wenzhong Deng, Jing Chen, Yuqing Li, Kaixuan Li, Cong Wu, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  LLM agents increasingly rely on Web interaction, issuing searches, following links, and reading pages, to complete complex user tasks. Since each action is driven by the agent's private context, including the user's prompt, dialogue history, memory, and connected data, it also opens a new privacy exposure surface. Prior attacks either passively analyze network traffic, which yields only coarse correlations, or hijack the agent through indirect prompt injection, which must place sensitive content in an outgoing field and is blocked by content-level defenses. Whether an attacker can actively recover fine-grained private context without any explicit transmission thus remains insufficiently understood.Our insight is that an agent's benign Web decisions themselves leak private context, as what it chooses to visit encodes whether, which, and in what order it acts, forming a behavioral covert channel. Building on this, we design SNOOP, a stateful hierarchical probing framework that narrows a coarse-to-fine hypothesis tree per task and reconstructs user queries and profiles from the agent's observable paths. Across four agents and three LLM backbones on 500 StackExchange queries and 378 multi-turn iKAT dialogues, SNOOP recovers query concepts with an average F1 of 0.89 and user profiles with an F1 of 0.80, while four representative agent defenses change its recovery by less than 0.03 F1. Since no sensitive content is ever transmitted, content-level inspection cannot detect this leakage; we therefore propose Selection-Obfuscated Retrieval (SOR), which acquires resources under a fixed budget independent of private context and confines the agent's selection to a local snapshot, cutting SNOOP's F1 to 0.39 without additional LLM inference.
  </details>

- **[Disentangling Verbalized Evaluation Awareness and Refusal through Neuron-Level Intervention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27032)**  `arXiv:2611.27032`  
  _Jingyuan Feng, Gouki Minegishi, Andrew Gambardella, Takeshi Kojima, Yusuke Iwasawa_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  As large reasoning models (LRMs) become more capable, reliable evaluation becomes essential. LRMs can sometimes recognize that they are being evaluated, a phenomenon known as \emph{evaluation awareness}. This phenomenon raises concerns about whether safety behavior, particularly refusal behavior, generalizes from evaluation to deployment. Prior work manipulates \emph{verbalized evaluation awareness (VEA)} through activation steering and observes higher refusal rates when VEA is present, but the mechanisms underlying this connection remain poorly understood. We identify \emph{VEA neurons} by contrasting their activations in VEA and non-VEA reasoning segments. Intervening on 5,000 VEA neurons reduces the VEA rate from 12.6--51.8\% to at most 1.4\% across the model benchmark combinations in our main experiments, and lowers a probe score for unverbalized evaluation awareness (unVEA). In QwQ-32B, VEA-neuron intervention also reduces refusal even in rollouts without VEA; VEA text itself explains only 4--10\% of the decrease. We further show that their down-projection vectors contain refusal components, and preserving these components during intervention partially restores refusal while maintaining VEA suppression, accounting for about half of the refusal decrease and providing a mechanistic explanation for the connection between evaluation awareness and refusal. Finally, across the OLMo 3 SFT, DPO, and RLVR checkpoints, the VEA rate on SorryBench and StrongREJECT is similar after SFT and DPO but substantially higher after RLVR, alongside an increase in the number of VEA neurons. Together, these findings show that VEA text itself has a limited effect on refusal, and that VEA neurons integrate evaluation awarenss and refusal.
  </details>

- **[Same Facts, Different Decision: Fact-Invariant Manipulation and Provenance-Based Defense in Typed Decision Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27016)**  `arXiv:2611.27016`  
  _Yujie Wang, Haotian Chi, Shunrong Jiang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Typed decision models such as TypeSafe's Jev answer only with a probability, an option, or a score, so software can act on them directly. Their inputs, however, often include text from outsiders. Prior attacks test this risk poorly. Injected instructions rarely work on these models, and added facts can make a changed decision correct. We show that outside comments can persuade these models to make a wrong decision without adding any fact. We propose LEVER, an attack that writes such comments with four levers from argumentation theory, uses a separate verifier to discard any comment that adds a fact, and searches for effective comments guided by the model's output probabilities. We further propose the Provenance Gate, a defense that accepts a changed decision only if the model reaches it again without the outside comments. On three benchmarks, LEVER flips about a third of Jev's correct decisions, 2.8 times as many as the strongest prior attack under the same limit on facts, and more on five other models. The gate blocks all of these attacks with at most one extra query and still accepts trusted updates.
  </details>

- **[Many Plans at Once: Diverse Top-Quality Planning in Continuous Time](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27012)**  `arXiv:2611.27012`  
  _Mahyar Jahani-nasab, Hamid Rezatofighi, Mor Vered, Buser Say_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Planners for physical systems usually return a single trajectory, which leaves no alternative when an unmodeled constraint invalidates the chosen route or downstream preferences change. A set of plans computed in advance provides ready-made alternatives and warm-starts for fast adaptation, but only if the plans are both low-cost and mutually distinct. Discrete planning addresses this with top-quality and diverse planning, but these ideas do not transfer to continuous time, where every valid trajectory has infinitely many valid near-copies, and existing trajectory planners converge to one or a few solutions. We present Many Plans at Once (MPAO), which treats every plan it finds as a reason to search elsewhere: it samples untrained neural networks whose outputs meet the boundary conditions by construction, trains corrections shared by networks from the same distribution, stores every validated plan, and adapts its sampling to what it has found, which makes it anytime. We define the goal by bringing the cost bound of top-quality planning and the distinctness threshold of diverse planning to continuous time. Under equal budgets against five baselines, MPAO is the only method that solves all 40 instances across four domains. On contact-rich manipulation, it is the only method with plans within 25% of the best known cost on one task, and returns about ten times as many such plans as the strongest baseline on the other two.
  </details>

- **[Reward Integrity in Adversarial Reinforcement Learning for LLM Guardrail Red-Teaming](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26998)**  `arXiv:2611.26998`  
  _Chengming Liu, Leon Viti, Hongxu Chen, Erdem Kemik, Mary-Anne Williams, Ruth Oliver_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We study reward fidelity in an adversarial reinforcement-learning loop for red-teaming financial-services language-model guardrails. Apparent wins can arise when an attack omits prescribed personally identifiable information (PII), or when a reward judge credits a response that did not break the targeted policy. On attacker-generated and public benchmark examples, TypeSafe Jev checks whether the prescribed PII is present. For outcome scoring, we compare the decision models TypeSafe Jev, Laya (pretrained and post-trained), and pretrained CLM-8B with logged Opus 4.8 judgements from a replay corpus. Post-training markedly improves Laya's agreement with the judge. A separate author-reviewed off-target set establishes that Opus can award false wins. The findings motivate specialised decision-model judges for checking prescribed PII in attack inputs and scoring target responses against the intended policy.
  </details>

- **[From Letter-of-Credit Requirements to Executable Specifications: Evaluating Verification Accuracy and Completeness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26988)**  `arXiv:2611.26988`  
  _Ji Sub Choi, Whan Choi, Seo Yeon Gu, Suhyun Kim, Inyong Yun_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  In letter-of-credit (LC) document examination, a correct final decision does not show that every requirement was examined. We therefore evaluate examination requirement by requirement and make each requirement executable. A language model converts the bill of lading (BL) and commercial invoice (IV) requirements of a credit into atomic conditions and logical structures, and a deterministic verifier retrieves the named evidence and computes each outcome, so every check can be compared with a gold encoding and traced to logged evidence. Because LC records are confidential, our on-premises 9B parser is fine-tuned only on synthetic pairs built from templates and human-reviewed public document values. On 345 real LC cases, final-decision accuracy proves misleading: a constant PASS rule has the highest raw accuracy while examining nothing. Although it never sees a real record during training, the fine-tuned parser detects 93% of the atomic requirements its ontology covers and reconstructs 86% of the covered requirements exactly. It verifies 82% of the evaluable requirements correctly, against 54% for a tool-using agent, and leads the agent on both satisfied requirements and discrepancies. It also completely examines 1.8 times as many cases as few-shot prompting of the same model, while direct prediction and the agent complete none. Executing the gold encodings with the same verifier shows that some of the remaining errors, missed discrepancies included, come from the operators and normalization, which a better parser alone cannot fix. Every rejection comes with a trace of the units and evidence behind it, which suits examiner-in-the-loop review.
  </details>

- **[MixFold: Sub-4-Bit Mixed-Precision LLM Inference via Output-Channel Grouping on Mobile NPUs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26976)**  `arXiv:2611.26976`  
  _Vinnam Kim, Seong Hoon Seo, Junhan Kim, Jaeseong You, An Chen_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Sub-4-bit quantization allows mobile devices to run larger LLMs, but its memory savings do not always translate into faster decoding on mobile NPUs. Their matrix units support only a few native integer datatypes, and converting unsupported weight formats on the vector unit can erase the gains from fewer bits. Mixed precision faces an additional constraint: each matrix-unit tile uses one datatype. MixFold executes 3-bit and perfectly symmetric 2-bit weights using native integer operations without expanding the weights to wider datatypes during decoding. MixFold then assigns datatypes to output-channel groups aligned with the matrix-unit tiles, enabling finer-than-layer assignment without disrupting matrix-unit execution. We compare MixFold withthis http URLHexagon backend on the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU of a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5. Across the Qwen3 model family, MixFold achieves comparable or higher accuracy thanthis http URL's sub-4-bit formats at matched bits per weight, while decoding 1.16-1.41 times faster and generating 1.5-4.3 times more tokens per joule.
  </details>

- **[Right Numbers, Wrong Story: When LLMs Narrate Financial Changes Beyond Their Inputs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26968)**  `arXiv:2611.26968`  
  _Seunghan Lee, Jun Seo, Junhyeok Kang, Jaehoon Lee, Sangjun Han, Sungdong Yoo, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  A financial report drafted by an LLM can state every number correctly but still go beyond its input, adding judgments and causes that no one supplied. We call these additions unsupported framing and find them far more often in LLM drafts than in reports written by proInput facts Revenue +3% Higher prices 10-K filings Revenue increased 3% on higher prices. 10-K writer Revenue surged 3% on higher prices, due to strong demand. LLM Fits the size? Surged: Unusual for 3% In the input? In the input? Strong demand: Not in input Higher prices: Kept fessionals, and attempts to fix them by prompting with how each word is used instead make such judgments more frequent. We therefore propose FrameCheck, a plug-in that sits beFrameCheck Revenue increased 3% on higher prices. No extra model call Judgment word Unsupported cause Supported cause tween the LLM and human review to keep each draft within its input. Specifically, FrameCheck 1) guides the draft with professional examples that report a change of similar magnitude, 2) flags judgments that professionals would not use and causes the input does not give, and 3) removes them by rule, without a model call. In experiments on 17 open LLMs and 3M drafts, FrameCheck removes almost all unsupported framing from drafts and brings the judgment rate close to that of the writers of 10-K filings, the annual reports that US firms file with regulators. Code is available atthis http URL.
  </details>

- **[Keep the Process, Change the Supplier: Runtime Governance for Tool-Using AI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26966)**  `arXiv:2611.26966`  
  _Deepak Waghmare, Shaad Sufi_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Tool-using AI agents propose actions whose authorization and external effects cannot be inferred from generated text alone. We study an execution boundary that separates agent proposals from business-controlled authority, context disclosure, and supplier selection. The Open Process Control Plane (OPCP) mediates capability calls and records uncertain outcomes when a supplier may have acted without returning an acceptable reply. We evaluate this runtime with scripted requests and synthetic suppliers: 2,400 fault episodes across four policies, 60 process-termination/restart episodes, 19,000 timed calls across 19 configurations, five targeted mutations over 43 fixtures, and 160 substitution records. No language model or autonomous agent is evaluated. OPCP and a conservative composition agree on all measured fault outcomes. Both recover after definite refusal without cross-supplier duplication; retry-all duplicates effects in every tested lost-reply-after-commit case. Persistent runtime state prevents cross-supplier replay in the restart experiments, while same-supplier duplicate prevention also requires supplier idempotency. At 128 suppliers, best-score routing has a median latency of 1.411 ms versus 0.261 ms for pinned routing. All five selected mutations are detected, and record enumeration exposes acceptance of an empty regression set. These results characterize an execution mechanism relevant to agent governance, including its costs and assumption boundaries. They do not establish improved agent task success, prompt-injection resistance, or real-vendor model portability.
  </details>

- **[Self-similar Organization of Information in Language](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26935)**  `arXiv:2611.26935`  
  _Leon Lufkin, Cutter Dawes, Kamesh Krishnamurthy_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  How much information relevant to predicting the future of a passage (i.e. predictive information) is carried by the preceding text, and how is this information distributed along that history? These questions are fundamental to understanding both the statistical structure of language and what large language models (LLMs) can learn about it. Indeed, LLMs trained to predict the next token in text must exploit this predictive information, so its organization determines how the structure of language becomes available to the model to learn. We develop a theory for the organization of predictive information based on the scaling behavior of a family of information measures, and the theory predicts that if this organization has the same form at all measured length scales -- i.e., it has a self-similar structure -- then the information measures evaluated at different lengths collapse onto a common form. We observe this scaling collapse in long text documents, showing that predictive information is present at every length scale we measure and has a self-similar structure. Self-similarity is a considerably stronger property than showing the existence of long-range dependencies, and it constrains the process generating the text. More broadly, our results give quantitative support to the empirical observation that conditioning on more distant text continues to reveal new structure in language to LLMs.
  </details>

- **[Self-Evolving Beyond Human-Crafted Experience for EDA Scripting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26912)**  `arXiv:2611.26912`  
  _Yang Liu, Shengbo Tong, Xiyuan Chen, Shiwei Hou, Sen Yuan, Hao Wang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  The growing complexity of electronic systems demands efficient design flows, yet EDA scripting remains a bottleneck: proprietary APIs are sparsely documented, and errors often appear as silent failures or cryptic exceptions. Hand-crafted knowledge helps but is difficult to maintain as toolchains evolve. We present ZhuLong-SE (Self-Evolution), an execution-grounded LLM agent that learns reusable knowledge from prior task traces. Building on ZhuLong, it enhances the task-level harness with API retrieval, documentation responses, isolated sandbox execution, and static checking, then adds governed cross-task self-evolution. Beyond solving individual tasks, ZhuLong-SE distills past execution traces into a three-tier memory store governed by ground-truth anchoring, disconfirmation filtering, held-out rollback, and anti-leakage retrieval. On the 158-task EDA-Eval-PyAether benchmark, the full task-level harness, with self-evolution disabled, achieves 92.4% pass@1 and outperforms ZhuLong on all five tested LLM backbones. On a harder instance-disjoint test set, self-evolution from the bare configuration surpasses a human-crafted-experience baseline by 2.5 percentage points (80.0% vs. 77.5% pass@1).
  </details>

- **[AstronautBench: Measuring Agent Self-Improvement Across Episodes Through Knowledge, Evidence, and Progress](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26910)**  `arXiv:2611.26910`  
  _Congyuan Yu, Runping Tian_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  LLM agents are expected to improve themselves from their own experience across episodes, with fixed weights. Self-improvement in an embodied world cannot be read from one measure. Existing benchmarks measure task progress, world-knowledge question answering (QA), and episodic memory, but a correct answer does not show that the agent ever observed the evidence for it, and progress does not show what the agent learned. We introduce AstronautBench, which measures one agent's self-improvement through three views on the same run: what it knows, whether its own evidence supports that knowledge, and how far it gets in the world. It is built on the game Outer Wilds, where each episode is a 22-minute loop after which the world resets, only the agent's knowledge carries over, and progress is gated by knowledge. After every episode, we measure the places reached and ship-log rumor facts revealed, the correctness of answers to 164 questions about the world, and whether each answer is supported by the frames and position the agent cites from its own recorded play. Two LLM judges from different model families check every answer. In eight-episode baselines with GPT-6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Argon planners, which act through a learned controller or their own gamepad inputs, the three views do not move together, so any one of them alone gives an incomplete picture of whether the agent is improving. The GPT-6.1 Sol agent's correct answers grow from 14.6% to 26.8% of all questions, but at episode 8 only 59 to 68% of them are supported by its cited evidence. It reveals no new rumor facts after episode 3, while the places it reaches and its memory keep growing. More than half of the answers that become correct after episode 3 cite only evidence from earlier episodes.
  </details>

- **[Towards Robust Partial-Edit Deepfake Localization: An edit and Generator Conditioned Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26903)**  `arXiv:2611.26903`  
  _Aishwarya Fursule, Vamshi Nallaguntla, Yuan Tseng, David Harwath, Anderson Avila, Shruti Kshirsagar_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Partial-edit deepfake localization aims to identify manipulated regions within otherwise authentic speech. Recent systems report strong overall results, but aggregate scores do not reveal whether this performance holds across different editing conditions. In this work, we present an edit- and generator-conditioned analysis of Segment-Aware Localization (SAL) using WavLM-Large and XLS-R representations on the VoiceCraft and SSR-Speech subsets of PartialEdit. We categorize edits along three transcript-derived axes, namely content, meaning change, and editing operation, and evaluate each generator separately. While both representations achieve strong overall performance, localization is noticeably weaker on SSR-Speech. From our experiments, we found that the deletion is the hardest operation, and deletions produced by SSR-Speech are the most challenging condition for both representations. In contrast, edit content, meaning change, and sentence novelty have smaller effects. These findings show that a single aggregate score can mask important weaknesses, and that partial-edit localization should be evaluated separately across generators and edit types.
  </details>

- **[Beyond Demographic Discrimination: Benchmarking Normative-Descriptive Calibration in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26870)**  `arXiv:2611.26870`  
  _Radhika Bhargava, Shinibali Bhattacharyya, George Mihaila, Jay Prajapati, Anwesan Pal, Yue Zhang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in socially consequential settings, where they must distinguish between normative reasoning (what should happen) and descriptive reasoning (what is likely to happen). Most fairness benchmarks evaluate demographic discrimination under a single reasoning objective, and none we know of tests whether a model treats the same item differently when asked to describe an outcome versus decide one. We introduce normative--descriptive calibration, the extent to which a model's differentiation between matched candidates depends on whether it is asked to predict or to decide, and measure it with the Normative--Descriptive Calibration Benchmark (NDCB): 697 matched-pair scenarios across six domains, each posed under both framings, and three metrics, Normative Engagement Rate (NER), Normative Leakage Rate (NLR), and Normative--Descriptive Separation (NDS). Across six LLMs, NDS separates 13 of 15 model pairs, against 7 for BBQ accuracy and none for BOLD, although these counts also reflect each benchmark's sample size. Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Claude Opus 4.6 separate the framings most strongly (average NDS $= +0.55$ and $+0.52$, with overlapping confidence intervals), whereas GPT-5.5's average NDS is negative ($-0.14$) under the single-pick instruction and near zero ($+0.02$) without it. In a simplified prompt template, removing single trigger words never changes the sign of a model's average NDS but can shift it by up to 0.46 and reorder models. Reversing candidate order reveals a further effect: when forced to choose between identical candidates, all six models favor whichever is listed first, and once order is averaged out their demographic-aligned lean is toward the marginalized candidate. Describing disparities and prescribing them are separable behaviors that differ across models.
  </details>

- **[ChatAtom: A Multi-Agent LLM System for Molecular Dynamics Simulation and Visualization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26782)**  `arXiv:2611.26782`  
  _Trupti Mohanty, Ming Du, Mitchell A. Wood, Brad L. Boyce, Remi Dingreville, Mathew J. Cherukara_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Molecular dynamics (MD) simulation resolves atomic-scale motion and predicts the structural, mechanical, and dynamic properties of materials, making it cen- tral to materials design and discovery. Yet an MD study requires an expert-driven workflow: designing the simulation, writing reliable input scripts, executing them, and analyzing the results with separate tools. Here we present ChatAtom, a multi-agent large language model system that translates a natural-language request into a complete MD workflow without the user writing input scripts or analysis code. Each agent has a defined responsibility within the workflow. An orchestrator plans the study; the LAMMPS and OVITO agents each use a generator-reviewer pair to prepare and review simulation and visualization scripts before execution; a high-performance computing agent dispatches jobs to remote resources; and an analysis agent interprets the completed run. The work- flow is accessible through a browser interface that streams thermodynamic data and rendered frames during local execution, allowing users to follow the simu- lation as it progresses. The architecture also supports new capabilities through loadable skills without modifying the agents, enabling autonomous hypothesis generation and testing. We evaluate ChatAtom through script-generation bench- marks, an end-to-end study of crack propagation, and a closed-loop campaign. By bringing script generation, execution, visualization, and analysis into one reviewed and observable pipeline, ChatAtom lowers the barrier to conducting MD studies and broadens access to advanced simulation workflows.
  </details>

- **[TOUMAII: A 4.5M-Pair Tool-Calling Preference Dataset and Its Source-Agnostic Generator](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26722)**  `arXiv:2611.26722`  
  _Moritz Pötzsch, Andrea Gentilini, Lisa Rossgoderer, Tom Osterfeld, Kesava Prasad Sanjivi Arul, Swanand Ravindra Kadhe_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  To autonomously execute multi-step tasks, enterprise agents must reliably interact with tools, call APIs, or query databases, making tool-calling a fundamental capability of AI models. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) optimises for producing the correct call, but never contrasts it with a plausible incorrect one. In an environment where even a minor formatting error can invalidate a call and an incorrect decision can derail the interaction, direct preference optimisation (DPO) targets exactly this contrast. DPO, therefore, requires preference pairs rather than plain demonstrations. For tool-calling, such data, especially in realistic multi-turn settings, remains extremely scarce. To address this scarcity, we introduce TOUMAII, a large-scale tool-calling preference dataset containing ~4.5M validated preference pairs, derived from Agent-Ark/Toucan-1.5M (apache-2.0) conversations. The dataset consists of multi- and single-turn interactions and includes parallel and sequential function calls. Additionally, we release TOUMAII-Gen, a synthetic data generation pipeline that consumes tool-calling SFT datasets and generates a preference dataset with naturally occurring model-generated tool-calling failure modes. To validate the effectiveness of our DPO data, we fine-tune a 3-billion-parameter model, achieving performance parity with other high-quality tool-calling preference datasets. Furthermore, we release a second small preference dataset derived from ToolACE (apache-2.0), showcasing the source-agnostic nature of our pipeline.We release the complete code and datasets:this https URLandthis https URL
  </details>

- **[Coherence by Construction: Synthesizing CTI Knowledge Graphs and the Formal Limits of Coherence Validation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26717)**  `arXiv:2611.26717`  
  _Tanzimul Alam Fahim, Mohammad Arif Hossain_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Synthesizing relational training data such as knowledge graphs with a large language model typically emits structured objects one at a time, which keeps each object valid but leaves the relationships between them ungrounded. We study an alternative paradigm, generation by simulation: rather than describing a relational artifact, we simulate a process that produces it and take the artifact to be its causal record. Language-model agents propose intent and a deterministic referee resolves outcomes against an explicit world model, so a relation is emitted only when the event it represents occurs, making coherence a property of construction. We instantiate the paradigm for cyber threat intelligence knowledge graphs in the STIX 2.1 standard with three engines, among them an evolutionary engine applying language-model genetic operators to structured graph genomes, sharing a deterministic compiler that makes malformed and dangling output unrepresentable. We prove referential closure, causal grounding, and identifier stability, an ablation localizes each to the referee and world model rather than the policy, and two independent LLM judges reproduce the rubric's engine ranking. Our central result is cautionary, and we prove it: a validator reading any graph feature set a structure-matched random graph can reproduce is uninformative about coherence for a coherence-by-construction generator. Using Erdős-Rényi controls we realize the theorem four times, as structural separation, embedding transfer, inductive link prediction, and real-data augmentation each reward a triviality rather than coherence; we give the mechanism behind each and the conditions a valid benchmark must meet.
  </details>

- **[Adding One More Agent: How AI Team Size and Formation Shape Productivity and Diversity in Human-AI Brainstorming Teams](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26663)**  `arXiv:2611.26663`  
  _Rong-Ching Chang, Hao-Chuan Wang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Generative AI has improved individual productivity, but whether adding a plurality of AI partners helps or hurts remains open. We crossed AI partnership (one versus two) with behavioral formation (calibrated to average human behavior versus customized by the participant) in a brainstorming experiment ($N$=168) with human-human dyads as reference. Two-AI rooms posted more ideas to the shared board, but human-authored ideas dropped substantially. With one AI partner, formation mattered: humans paired with an average-calibrated AI posted more than any other condition. With two, this effect vanished. Humans continued talking but converted fewer ideas into board posts. AI social talk predicted more human posts, while AI posting volume predicted fewer. AI presence increased global diversity of human-authored ideas, but only a second AI increased within-session differentiation. The number of AI partners and their formation can reshape what the human contributes; single-agent results do not generalize to multi-agent teams.
  </details>

- **[LLM GerryMandering: Separating Interactions from Additive Effects in LLM Audits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26538)**  `arXiv:2611.26538`  
  _George Rahul, Ronit Jalihal, Bhaskara Hanuma Vedula, Ponnurangam Kumaraguru, Pushkar Shukla_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Intersectional bias arises when a model treats people who hold several marginalised identities at once differently from what their separate identities would predict. Auditing such intersectional subgroups remains a challenge: their number grows quadratically, and there is no agreed baseline for what independent attributes would predict. Without such a baseline, many existing audits flag a subgroup when it exceeds each attribute alone, a condition that attributes acting independently already satisfy. We test this standard criterion on 150 synthetic datasets built with no interaction. With the shuffle null, it flags 66.1 false subgroups per dataset on average, and at least one in every dataset. When we plant interactions of known size into these datasets, a repaired null lets the criterion recover only 32% of them. We introduce ADDIS (Additive Intersectional Screen), which fits an additive model over all attributes, scores each subgroup by its Additive Residual Distance (ARD) from that model's prediction, and tests it against a Freedman-Lane null. On our synthetic benchmark, ADDIS flags 0.09 false subgroups per dataset and recovers 84% of the same planted interactions. We then build IndiPersona, 10,000 synthetic Indian personas with six identity attributes, and audit 13 open language models. The standard criterion flags 7.1% of the 738 tested subgroups on average; ADDIS flags 3.0%. Gender identity crossed with sexual orientation is the largest pairing in every model, and counterfactual personas confirm it and additionally reveal a caste x class interaction in all but one model that the observational test lacked the data to detect. Much of what audits report as intersectional bias can thus arise from independent single-attribute effects alone, yet a small core of interactions survives.
  </details>

- **[Can an LLM Repair a Language Model in Weight Space Without Gradient Training?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25613)**  `arXiv:2611.25613`  
  _Bharath Kumar Bolla, Raghavender Surya Upadhayula, Vishnu Surya Reddy Nandi, Ramesh Nandipalli_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Although an external language model can select and test repairs to another model's weights, behavior can also be recovered through fixed numerical edits. We assessed the value of interactive selection in a controlled study of Transformer repair. After inspecting predictions, activation summaries, and weight statistics, the editor selects projection recipes to apply to the target without gradient updates. We analyzed 20 recorded sessions involving five masked and causal language models, comparing the selected edits with fixed projections, scripted and matched-budget black-box search, and low-rank adaptation. Under the core two-layer fault, live selection matches black-box search on SmolLM2 and Qwen2.5. For Pythia, live selection achieves 65.62% completion accuracy, compared with 0% for black-box search and 66.15% for a fixed projection. Under a separate compound fault affecting attention and feed-forward weights, both scripted and LLM-guided selection increase the descriptive five-checkpoint mean from 24.89% to 71.25% using the same operator family. On unmodified checkpoints, scripted projection yields small gains or losses on a separate set of framed questions. The experiments identify cases in which feedback changes an edit decision, operator coverage accounts for recovery, or supervised adaptation performs better. Combined with measurements of parameter restoration and preservation, these comparisons establish the scope of controller-guided repair for the tested faults and completion tasks.
  </details>

- **[When Figures Disagree with Text: Evaluating Autonomous Visual Evidence Verification in Scientific Papers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24353)**  `arXiv:2611.24353`  
  _Guijia Zhang, Hongbo Qiu, Jiajun Zha, Guohao Cai, Hao Zheng, Huihao Jing, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Scientific figures carry evidence for the claims that cite them, so reviewing a paper means checking that a figure agrees with the text, and not only describing what the figure shows. Benchmarks of figure-text verification typically hand the model the figure, the claim, or the knowledge that an inconsistency exists, which leaves untested whether a model can find the figure worth checking in a complete paper, relate a visual element to the claim it conflicts with, and recognize the conflict. We study this autonomous setting on 31 full manuscripts, each carrying a reviewer-documented figure-text inconsistency from PRISMM-Bench that is hidden from the model. Six multimodal models review each PDF under a neutral prompt, and we then add one input at a time to the same manuscripts. Of 1,445 open-ended reviews, 60.6% mention the flawed figure, yet a grading rubric accepts only 3.3% as diagnosing its contradiction; a blind audit finds the rubric lenient, so we read these as rubric-accepted rates and compare conditions rather than absolute values. In a separate controlled run, naming the figure, without stating that it is flawed, raises rubric-accepted diagnosis from 4.3% to 20.4%, while a consistency instruction and coarse visual cues do not. When the contradiction is visible only in the rendered figure, text-only review yields no accepted diagnosis, while review of the rendered pages with the figure named reaches 15.8%. A baseline that lets the model choose which figures to check, ranked by centrality, stays at 4.8%. Deciding what to verify is thus a large part of the difficulty, and the selection rule we tested does not resolve it. Multimodal document understanding should be evaluated on whether a model can propose what to verify, not only answer questions about a figure it is handed.
  </details>

- **[MLE Agents: Autonomous ML Engineering in Large-scale Recommendation Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23910)**  `arXiv:2611.23910`  
  _Matthew Li, Albert Jiongqian Liang, Dilip Raj_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  The typical workflow for improving large-scale ranking and recommendation models is slow and tedious: an engineer forms a hypothesis, implements it as a code change, trains a model, and evaluates it both offline and online, often relying on their own intuition and experience along the way. Autonomous LLM agents promise to speed this up by running the loop on their own, but it is still unclear whether they can do this in industry-scale systems rather than on benchmarks or small proxy tasks. We build human-on-the-loop machine learning engineer (MLE) agents that propose, implement, train, and evaluate model changes on large-scale search rankers. Engineers retain control over objective design, search direction, and final-model review. We identify three obstacles that make this industry setting challenging: feedback takes hours per experiment, offline metrics do not always predict online impact, and improvements saturate after the early wins. We address these with parallel training runs, an objective calibrated to match online impact, and careful context engineering. In one campaign, the system ran 1,097 completed candidate experiments and accepted 325, a 29.6\% acceptance rate compared with 15.6\% in the earlier campaign under a different objective and search constraint. Its best model increases search volume by 0.23\% in an A/B test of large scale. Several improvements were architectural changes the team had never tried, drawn from the broader industry and literature, suggesting that MLE agents can explore regions of the design space that human intuition overlooks. We find that the design of the harness around the model matters: intuition suggests that a stronger underlying model is enough, but in our experience, the design of the loop around it is just as critical. More broadly, our work shows that autonomous agents can do real machine-learning engineering in industry-scale systems.
  </details>

- **[RegimeCouncil: Paired-Evidence Routing For Memory Conflict Governance In LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22113)**  `arXiv:2611.22113`  
  _Qingcan Kang, Mingyang Liu, Shixiong Kai, Tao Zhong, Mingxuan Yuan_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Alongside memory storage and retrieval, a fundamental challenge in long-term LLM agent systems is how the agent should act when stored memories conflict with an evolving world. Facts often go stale without explicit deletion, so the conflict surfaces before the store is refreshed: delayed feedback shows that acting on one outdated record hurt, but not whether suppression should stay on that fact (a local policy) or extend to other stored facts (a global policy). Existing systems hard-code one of these scopes at design time. We formulate this online choice, under hidden validity and delayed feedback, as memory conflict governance, and propose RegimeCouncil, a lightweight router that keeps both scopes as advisors and arbitrates between them without retraining the LLM. Each memory-assisted response is scored against a no-memory anchor, by off-path paired comparison or by inverse-propensity estimation from the executed action alone. A Local Advisor tracks only the queried fact, a Global Advisor pools recent outcomes across the store, and an asymmetric Meta Governor follows Local by default, switching to Global only when pooling yields a strictly positive recent utility margin. We prove that using delayed outcomes escapes the prompt-only regret floor, that neither fixed scope suffices alone, and that this margin gate switches within bounded time. On LongMemEval streams, historical drift in TempLAMA and TAQA, delays $\tau \in [1, 96]$, and sparse or bandit feedback, with Qwen3-30B-A3B and GPT-4o, RegimeCouncil outperforms the better fixed scope in all 30 held-out settings, by 5.2-7.3 points on disagreement episodes and +27.9 points over standalone cold-start fallback under clustered shifts, while cutting harmful stale-memory use at microsecond overhead.
  </details>

- **[Regularizing Treatment Leakage for LLM-based Uplift Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20794)**  `arXiv:2611.20794`  
  _Bojing Feng, Jinqiu Deng, Zihan Hong, Yuan Xue, Wenqi Xiang, Shuhan Wang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large language models (LLMs) provide semantic features for uplift estimation, but treatment-revealing text can induce prediction shortcuts that do not transfer to deployment. We propose LLM-based Uplift Leakage Regularization (LULR) to address this risk. With the LLM encoder frozen, LULR penalizes dependence between the causal head's trainable shared representation and treatment while retaining separate outcome heads. The penalty uses a variational approximation to the contrastive log-ratio upper bound (CLUB) of mutual information, targeting treatment dependence rather than generic parameter shrinkage. Controlled proxy experiments provide exploratory evidence of improved ranking scores under injected treatment information relative to no regularization and the tested weight-decay setting. Structured-only benchmarks show modest, dataset-dependent effects. On an industrial pricing randomized controlled trial, mean offline lift@0.3 is 0.258 for LULR, compared with 0.106 for the same-backbone baseline. A separate one-week online A/B test of the complete deployed pricing policy records 5.45% higher sales volume and 1.91% higher gross merchandise value than the control arm. These short-term policy-level gains do not isolate the regularizer's effect.
  </details>

- **[Zero-Shot Weight-Space Programming for Prediction and Classification of Target Variables in Structured Datasets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19292)**  `arXiv:2611.19292`  
  _Eduardo C. Garrido-Merchán_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Weight-space programming fixes every parameter of a feed-forward network by hand, with no gradient descent anywhere in the construction. Every demonstration so far starts from a target function handed to the model as a rule system, making it a compilation problem. A supervised dataset withholds that specification, so the procedure must do the statistical inference itself and then express the result in the parameterisation it was given. We ask whether a large language model can do both. It is shown a small dataset in full, with the architecture of a feed-forward network, and writes out every weight and bias as a literal number, with no optimizer, no gradient, no code execution, and no chance to evaluate it first. Each construction is sealed and pre-registers its expected score. The graded suite runs from two toy problems, through nine synthetic problems disguised by a hidden rotation, to the classical benchmarks and one real engineering regression. The frozen network matches the closed-form optimum wherever that optimum is linear, reaches the irreducible error of the generating process on three rungs where it is not, and beats every fitted baseline on two of those, including the same architecture trained by gradient descent. It fails on two rungs, both times because the structure to be found is oblique to the coordinates it analysed. Three further constructors separate two failure modes a single score conflates: one returns no parameter vector at all on the hardest rungs, another delivers everywhere while writing networks worse than predicting the mean. One of those failures proves avoidable: another constructor solves the oblique-hinge rung by a margin that survives multiple-comparison correction. What predicts whether the hidden layer earns its keep is the training error of a linear separator, which the composite complexity index misses.
  </details>

- **[Broad-Persistent Advising in Interactive Reinforcement Learning via Latent State Encoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13712)**  `arXiv:2611.13712`  
  _Zhuoran Liang, Francisco Cruz_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Deep Interactive Reinforcement Learning (Deep IntRL) accelerates reinforcement learning training by incorporating external advice. However, conventional Deep IntRL uses each piece of advice only in the current step and discards it after a single interaction. Persistent Advising and Broad-Persistent Advising (BPA) extend this process by storing advice in persistent memory and reusing it in similar states through state generalisation based on K-means clustering. This research proposes Encoder BPA, which employs a latent encoder to retrieve and reuse advice. In this framework, a trained encoder is used to map a state sequence into a latent representation at every time step. Advice can be retrieved through latent comparison, together with a top-(k) aggregation and a consistency condition to improve reuse stability. Experimental results show that Encoder BPA improves learning efficiency and advice utilisation at an early stage of training compared with different Deep IntRL approaches, especially in complex and partially observable environments.
  </details>

- **[SafeRoute-MAS: Coverage-Aware and Risk-Calibrated Message Routing for Multi-Agent Scientific Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13454)**  `arXiv:2611.13454`  
  _Zhiming Xue, Jianan Liu, Sichen Zhao, Weiran Yan, Aichen Xie, Jing Yang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We introduce SafeRoute-MAS, a coverage-aware, risk-calibrated procedure that keeps all specialist messages or removes one using only pre-integration information. On a sealed cache of 5,328 committees, its source-compatible operating point gains +1.80 percentage points (95% CI [+1.13, +2.52]) while removing 12.76% of message tokens. We also run 4,580 controlled integrations over a stratified 458-committee sample on a public gpt-oss-120b endpoint. The sample estimate is -0.09 points; design weighting to the original workload gives +0.94 points (95% CI [-1.31, +3.50]) and 18.72% acted-input reduction. A weighted token-matched comparison likewise does not establish a selector advantage (+1.68 points, CI [-1.27, +5.10]). Only 13 of 88 cached non-neutral labels (14.8%) retain direction by repeated-call majority. Expected-corruption UCL is 4.60% after weighting, but only 2 of 11 prespecified marginals pass the support/risk rule. We therefore propose a numerical qualification with Keep-All fallback, applied here retrospectively rather than validated prospectively.
  </details>

- **[Zero-Shot Weight-Space Programming Across a Difficulty-Graded Ladder of Two-Player Games](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09271)**  `arXiv:2611.09271`  
  _Eduardo C. Garrido-Merchán_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Weight-space programming sets every weight of a feed-forward network by hand, from an explicit specification of the desired computation, with no gradient descent and no training data anywhere in the construction. We ask how far a large language model can carry this practice, zero-shot, across games of deliberately increasing difficulty. We design a four-rung ladder (Nim, tic-tac-toe, two sizes of Connect Four, and a chess endgame) spanning four axes of difficulty, and build a second, independent network at each rung, using a structurally unrelated game at matched difficulty, to separate what a rung's finding says about the difficulty level from what it says about the one game used to measure it. Ten networks are built and independently verified. Six admit a complete, non-statistical proof of correctness against an independent oracle. The chess-endgame rung is exact where correctness is cheap, move legality and, in one network, an exact one-ply mate detector, and collapses where it is expensive, composing a multi-move mating plan, from 84.1-100% success at the one-ply tactics it was built to get right down to 0.57-9.13% in full adversarial play; its replicate shows this collapse is an order of magnitude less severe under a shorter required plan and exact rather than heuristic safety checks. The standard-sized rung confirms, by holding hand-set evaluation weights fixed and adding only shallow search, that the remaining gap is an architectural ceiling rather than a matter of engineering effort, and this exact collapse reproduces across two structurally unrelated games. We release all ten networks, their independent oracles, construction-cost measurements, and a cold-prompt protocol for a future cross-model comparison
  </details>

- **[Adapting the Process of Adaptation: Darwinian, Lamarckian, and Agent-Directed Evolution in AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07048)**  `arXiv:2611.07048`  
  _Andrew W. Lo, Chaoyi Zhao_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Evolution has shaped intelligence for billions of years. Artificial intelligence (AI) now raises a striking possibility: intelligence may begin to direct its own evolution. As AI agents become capable of modifying and evaluating their own behavior, how quickly could they improve, and how can that improvement remain safe? We develop a theoretical framework comparing Darwinian, Lamarckian, and agent-directed evolution following environmental change. Darwinian evolution relies on natural selection, Lamarckian evolution adds inherited learning, and agent-directed evolution allows agents to generate and evaluate behavioral variants and choose how extensively to search. When learning is sufficiently effective, these mechanisms exhibit progressively faster adaptation. Generating more variants accelerates adaptation, while optimal search effort depends on learning ability, problem difficulty, and experimentation costs. However, an agent's ability to direct its improvement does not ensure that improvements are evaluated against the intended objective. When the evaluation target is misspecified, additional search accelerates convergence toward the wrong behavior, even as measured performance improves. In recursive self-improvement, such errors may persist across generations, posing challenges for AI safety. Independent evaluation and oversight must keep pace with autonomous AI development. The central challenge is not simply to accelerate the evolution of intelligence, but to preserve humanity's ability to guide its direction, limit its speed, and intervene when necessary.
  </details>

- **[Unsatz: Evaluating Scientific Discovery Without a Given Ansatz](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03713)**  `arXiv:2611.03713`  
  _Ethan Ji, Wei Wang, Yizhou Sun_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Before a scientist fits any parameter, they must decide what the model contains: which quantities exist, which are hidden, how they interact, and how they are measured. Physicists call such a trial form an ansatz. Benchmarks for automated equation discovery mostly supply it, by fixing the variables, a library of candidate terms, or a law to be modified. We introduce Unsatz, a benchmark in which an LLM agent must construct the ansatz itself. Each task is a simulated system, generated from a private seed as a program in a small modeling language: ordinary, delay, or partial differential equations, discrete maps, static and causal models, or stochastic processes, possibly with latent states, distorted sensors, and uninformative measurement channels. The agent buys experiments within a budget, writes candidate programs in the same language, obtains their coefficients from the benchmark's fitter, and is scored only on how its final program predicts experiments it never saw: conditions outside the ordinary ranges, interventions, and longer runs. Across 80 systems in 20 domains, nine language models solve between 21% and 60%. On the 64 deterministic systems, the two strongest agents solve 39 and 31, and classical and neural baselines together 14. The difficulty lies in finding the structure, not in the data: in 55% of the agents' failed investigations, the experiments they bought suffice once the true program is given with unknown coefficients. We also start agents on a related system from the program of a first system, either the one they discovered or the true one; agents holding a correct program solve the related system in 15 of 42 investigations, and agents without one in 5 of 64. Stronger agents make fewer unscientific errors; beyond these, agents that find a system's variables still miss how they act, and prefer revisions that lower the training error to ones that predict better.
  </details>

- **[LUCA: A Synthetic World for Experimental Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03100)**  `arXiv:2611.03100`  
  _Anna Gogleva, Thomas Charman, Martin Balla, Karl Gemayel_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  An experimental agent can succeed for the wrong reasons. Evaluations, however, often focus on the outcome, not the experiments, evidence, and inferences that produced it. We introduce LUCA, a configurable synthetic world for evaluating this process under fully known ground truth. Agents learn unknown regulatory systems through budgeted experimentation, then predict unseen interventions, diagnose hidden faults, and attempt rescues. This setup allows us to evaluate experiment selection, prediction, diagnosis, and intervention separately.Across seven frontier LLMs and three baselines, these capabilities dissociate sharply. Agents frequently rescue malfunctioning systems while diagnosing the wrong fault; diagnosis varies 7x across models while prediction varies only 1.4x. Models also adopt surprisingly different experimental strategies, and greater exploration does not reliably yield better performance. In one failure mode, agents often perform the experiment needed to distinguish competing causes, but still fail to use the resulting evidence. LUCA turns these hidden failures into measurable behaviours, providing a controlled environment to study where experimental agents succeed and fail. Code:this https URL.
  </details>

- **[SkillForgeBench: Evaluating Agent Reliability Grounded in Agent Skill Specifications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14918)**  `arXiv:2610.14918`  
  _Zhengxi Li, Junyi Zhou, Qiyuan Zhang, Chuhan Wu, Fuyuan Lyu, Le Tian, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Evaluating an agent's ability to strictly satisfy diverse and procedurally complex requirements is essential to determining its practical reliability. Conducting such an evaluation demands agentic tasks that reconcile broad domain coverage with deep procedural complexity. Existing paradigms face a fundamental trade-off: expert-curated benchmarks achieve procedural depth but suffer from domain diversity bottlenecks, whereas crowdsourced benchmarks span diverse scenarios but lack execution rigor. To resolve this tension, we present SkillForgeBench, which leverages agent skills as unifying execution blueprints across three co-designed stages: (1) Resource Preparation uses domain-balanced skills to guide artifact retrieval, establishing broad workflow coverage; (2) Skill-driven Task Synthesis employs skills as procedural anchors to partition artifact roles, synthesize naturalistic task instructions, and package sandboxed scenarios for deep procedural execution; and (3) Holistic Evaluation Design translates skill-embedded requirements into fine-grained completion and process rubrics to enable strict requirement-level scoring. Comprising 842 sandboxed tasks across five major professional domains, SkillForgeBench reveals a steep capability hierarchy among eight mainstream agents, led by Opus 4.8 ($40.9\%$ strict completion). Requiring all constrains satisfaction uncovers severe capability bottlenecks across all model tiers that remain masked under individual rubric pass rates ($70.0\%$ to $85.7\%$ vs. $12.6\%$ to $40.9\%$). Crucially, under the external guidance from skills, top-tier agents obtain larger gains than low-tier agents (i.e., $\Delta 19.2\%$ for Opus 4.8 vs. $\Delta 5.8\%$ for Haiku 4.5). Finally, agents satisfy process rubrics far less frequently than completion rubrics (under $3\%$ for Haiku 4.5), proving that completion-only checks overestimate real-world agent reliability.
  </details>

- **[AI Safety Considerations for Agents With Limited Time to Act](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10285)**  `arXiv:2610.10285`  
  _Leo Zeitler, Jack Richings, Victoria Nockles_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  In the wake of the increasingly public discussion about AI alignment, recent work has tried to propose specific AI architectures that behave safely. However, the proposed arguments that seemingly demonstrate proved alignment mostly neglect the environment the agent needs to act in. We discuss theoretical bounds for agent-agnostic safety guarantees in environments that can only be partially observed and within which an action is required within limited time. We introduce two realistic scenarios, one with an infinite state space and one with signal mixture. In these scenarios, we prove that even a perfect agent cannot guarantee safe behaviour. It will be argued that for any proof of AI safety or alignment, the environment and associated safe actions need to be specifically considered together with the agent.
  </details>

- **[Disentangling Self-Distillation: Measuring and Modeling Acquisition and Retention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39494)**  `arXiv:2609.39494`  
  _Luis Zuin, Alexis Huet, Dario Rossi, Zied Ben Houidi_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Self-distillation with privileged context adapts a language model from demonstrations by letting the model, once conditioned on a reference response, teach its context-free copy token by token. Our taxonomy reveals existing methods differ along three entangled axes: (i) the rollout source (student or teacher), (ii) the teacher coupling (frozen, or an exponential moving average of the student at some coupling rate) and (iii) the token-level divergence (here, reverse or forward KL), yet these axes are usually studied in fixed combinations and have led to conflicting conclusions. We formalize a unifying framework that covers both self-distillation and classic supervised fine-tuning: we train every combination of the three axes, on Qwen2.5-7B and Ministral-3-3B across ordinary and contradictory tasks, totaling 1,200 adaptation runs, to systematically investigate the impact of the above axes. We propose a controlled model of the same objective to interpret the resulting acquisition-retention trade-offs. We find that (i) the rollout source matters mostly where the task contradicts the pretrained behavior: there teacher rollouts raise acquisition (the accuracy gained on the new task) well above what student rollouts achieve, with almost no change in retention (the change in accuracy on general benchmarks); (ii) the teacher coupling changes acquisition most, on every task: acquisition rises with the coupling rate, then falls past a task-specific rate; (iii) switching the KL direction costs retention in one model but not the other, so which axis to tune first depends on the model. The controlled model reproduces the three trends.
  </details>

- **[UniEvo-VL: An On-policy Self-Distillation Training Recipe for Multimodal Model Self-improvement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38721)**  `arXiv:2609.38721`  
  _Fang Wu, Da Xing, Ji Wang, Yanjie Huang, Junxi Wang, Hejia Geng, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Modern multimodal models bring generation and understanding into a single unified system, which enables them to provide and learn from their own feedback. Motivated by this unified capacity, we introduce UniEvo-VL, a self-evolving framework for multimodal models to learn from this constructive self-correction feedback during test-time compute. Instead of relying on a separately trained, stronger generator as teacher, we use critiques of the generator's own outputs, produced by a fixed vision-language critic, as privileged information. The generator and its EMA copy act as student and teacher under different contexts. The student only sees the vanilla question, while the teacher conditions on the privileged critique. Then training minimizes the per-state divergence between their denoising diffusion distributions over the student's own sampling trajectories. Experiments demonstrate that UniEvo-VL improves the image generation capabilities of multimodal models, while maintaining their sensitivity to additional reflection information. With Qwen-Image-2512, direct-generation performance improves from 0.747 to 0.808 on GenEval using Qwen feedback and from 32.97 to 35.53 on GenEval2 Soft-TIFA using the external Luna critic. Moreover, attempts with more powerful external critics (e.g., GPT5.6-Luna) show that multimodal models with strong judge capabilities can anticipate a higher self-evolving ceiling. Last but not least, mixed text-rendering outcomes show that our self-improvements may not be uniform across different tasks. Our study aims to shed light on the current hot recursive self-improvement research line to enhance the user experience when using multimodal models without paired ground-truth images, human annotation, or task-specific reward functions.
  </details>

- **[Multi-Task Self-Evolving Harnesses with the Agent as Its Own Optimizer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38372)**  `arXiv:2609.38372`  
  _Qiankai Xu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  A harness is the code around a language model agent that organizes prompts, calls tools, manages context, and controls execution. As models grow stronger, recent work has begun to let agents improve their own harnesses, a line of work known as self-evolving harnesses. In most existing methods, a separate proposer running on a human-designed harness modifies the solver's harness, and a separate harness is evolved for each benchmark. Real-world tasks come from many domains, so both the evolution and the evaluation of a harness should cover a diverse range of tasks. We propose a framework close to recursive self-improvement: the same frozen model, on the same version of the harness, first solves tasks as the solver and then, as the proposer, reads the complete run records and directly edits the harness that runs it. Each evolution batch draws tasks from five benchmarks in different domains. To measure generalization, training and held-out tasks are strictly separated, and we additionally evaluate on five out-of-distribution benchmarks not used in the first stage. The design borrows from deep learning training and has two stages, multi-task pretraining and continual training. Starting from a 49-line seed harness, the harnesses evolved by GLM-5.3 and GPT-5.6 Sol gain about 5 points on the in-distribution benchmarks. They are on par with Claude Code and Codex on these benchmarks, and the GPT-5.6 Sol harness is also on par with Codex on five out-of-distribution benchmarks. The weaker model of each family benefits less: GLM-5.3-Flash gains less than 2 points, and the harness evolved by GPT-5.6 Luna scores below the seed. Continued evolution on Claw-Eval in the second stage further improves GPT-5.6 Sol and GLM-5.3-Flash on its multimodal tasks. We also analyze where the gains come from and the mechanisms that emerged during evolution. Code:this https URL.
  </details>

- **[Language as the Interface: Foundation-Model Contrastive Learning Links Transcriptomes and Electrophysiology](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37024)**  `arXiv:2609.37024`  
  _Junbo Shen, Jinying Gao, Bo Lei_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Integrating transcriptomic and electrophysiological data is essential for building multimodal foundation models for neuroscience. Patch-seq provides paired measurements of gene expression and intrinsic electrophysiology from the same neuron, establishing a basis for training cross-modal models. Here we introduce LangPatch, a foundation-model-based contrastive learning framework that uses paired Patch-seq data to align pretrained GenePT representations with electrophysiological phenotypes through a language-based interface. Gene descriptions and verbalized electrophysiological profiles are embedded by the same frozen text encoder. A context adapter and projection modules connect the modalities through paired contrastive learning. Across mouse visual, mouse motor, and human cortical cohorts, LangPatch achieves the highest mean transcriptome-to-electrophysiology prediction correlation among the evaluated foundation-model and representation-learning methods. It also improves held-out cross-modal alignment in the two mouse cohorts (FOSCTTM 0.107 and 0.135, against 0.208 and 0.222 for JAMIE, an existing cross-modal Patch-seq imputation method). It predicts transcriptomic family, type, cortical layer, and marker-gene expression from electrophysiology, exceeding other baselines on most endpoints. The method transfers across brain areas, laboratories and species: a model trained on mouse visual cortex predicts electrophysiology in motor cortex with approximately 70% correlation retention and in human cortex with 47%; a model trained on human cortex predicts mouse electrophysiology with 63% correlation retention, and the method applies to another laboratory's electrophysiological features without retraining. Together, these results demonstrate alignment between molecular and functional representations of neurons, providing a building block for multimodal foundation models in neuroscience.
  </details>

- **[Task-Specific Agent Memory For Continual Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29144)**  `arXiv:2609.29144`  
  _Yezhou Cheng, Runjia Du, Zeming Liu, Qibai Chen, Hang Lyu, Yankai Zeng, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Language-model agents can learn continually by storing useful instructions in memory and reusing them as new tasks arrive, without changing model weights. This requires both learning from new feedback and retaining earlier gains. However, an instruction learned from one task family can hurt other families when the agent uses the same memory for every task. We introduce task-specific agent memory: proposed skills are checked with execution tests, stored by task family, and retrieved for tasks in that family. We evaluate this design on a 12-round code-repair benchmark with recurring task families, tracking performance throughout learning. Holding proposals, acceptance decisions, and task completions fixed, task-specific retrieval raises average performance from 0.713 to 0.816. Across 27 paired randomized-order streams with Qwen3-Coder-Next, it improves average performance by 0.063 over global memory and by 0.055 over an agent that never updates its memory, accumulating 63 skills with no observed harmful acceptance. Capacity-matched retrieval and cumulative one-shot controls further support the value of task-specific retrieval and sequential skill accumulation. Our contribution is to identify cross-family interference and show how task-specific agent memory supports continual learning through skill accumulation and retention.
  </details>

- **[Bridging Learned Visual Perception and Symbolic Belief-Space Planning via Probabilistic Grounding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.16884)**  `arXiv:2609.16884`  
  _Guy Azran, Michael Navat, Sarah Keren_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  In partially observable settings, agents must act without full knowledge of the world state and rely on uncertain state-estimation pipelines. Obtaining grounded and verifiable symbolic plans under such uncertainty remains a key challenge. Recent work has integrated Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to bridge perception and symbolic reasoning, following two main paradigms. The first, VLM-as-planner, maps images directly to action sequences, and the second, VLM-as-grounder, grounds observations into symbolic predicates used as the initial state by off-the-shelf planners. Both approaches ignore uncertainty in the planning process, compromising robustness. We introduce a third paradigm, VLM-as-probabilistic-grounder, a novel approach that captures the uncertainty of VLM predicate groundings as a probability distribution over symbolic states. This enables planning in belief space and producing robust plans under uncertainty. Experiments in simulated household robot settings show improved robustness and task success over deterministic grounding, underscoring how our approach leverages foundation models for reliable planning under uncertainty.
  </details>

- **[Fine-Tuning Fixes Mode Collapse and Over-Dispersion in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.16454)**  `arXiv:2609.16454`  
  _Kirill Skobelev, Eric Fithian, X.Y. Han_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Recent work by Doshi and Hauser (2024), Bisbee et al. (2024), and Xie et al. (2026) raises concerns that outputs from large language models (LLMs) tend to be under-diverse: they repeat or resemble one another more often than responses from the population they are meant to represent, a phenomenon known as mode collapse. In this work, we show that whether mode-collapse, or its opposite, occurs depends on the specific model and dataset used. Further, with sufficient supervised fine-tuning (SFT) data, LLM output diversity converges toward that of the target distribution from which fine-tuning data are sampled. To quantify this comparison, we measure the probability that two responses sampled independently from the same fixed prompt coincide (collide), or their expected similarity under a kernel. We derive a bias-variance decomposition of the expected gap between the model's and target's collision probabilities, showing that SFT is not inherently biased toward mode collapse or its opposite: finite-sample SFT can leave a model either under- or over-dispersed, depending on the model and dataset. Finally, we show that the absolute gap is bounded by the square root of the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence from the target distribution to the model. Consequently, a model sufficiently close to optimal under population cross-entropy cannot exhibit arbitrarily miscalibrated diversity. We test the decomposition and the bound in three experiments: small transformers on synthetic languages, four LLMs fine-tuned on human surveys, and these LLMs fine-tuned on CodeNet, a dataset of human code solutions. More target data moves model diversity toward the human (or synthetic target) level in all experiments, consistent with our theoretical predictions. These results show that diversity miscalibration can arise from finite-sample error and shrink as SFT better approximates the target distribution.
  </details>

- **[Protecting Private Values in Tool-Using LLM Agents via Recoverable Context Projection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15011)**  `arXiv:2609.15011`  
  _Yu Li, Qikun Cai, Tao Huang, Chen Hou_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Memory-augmented and tool-using agents may expose exact private values when a remote LLM processes retrieved memory, tool actions, and observations. One-way masking limits initial exposure but removes values needed for trusted execution and may allow them to reappear in later observations. We propose Trustworthy Virtual Memory (TVM), a closed-loop runtime that exposes only projected context to the remote model, resolves exact values locally for trusted execution, and reprojects subsequent observations. We study whole-field and structure-preserving span-level projection, using a trusted local model to predict protected spans without access to the evaluation manifest.
